01_input.question: How many numbers does the computer store for the 35-character prompt about Los Angeles?
options: It stores the meaning, not numbers
01_input.why: Plain English letters are one byte each. Words and meaning do not exist yet at this stage.
01_input.predict: Your prompt has 35 characters. How many numbers does the computer store for it: fewer, exactly 35, or more?

02_tokenizer.question: Why is a rare word like Reykjavik split into several tokens while weather is one token?
options: Byte Pair Encoding only glues together pairs it saw OFTEN in its training text
02_tokenizer.why: Merges are learned by frequency. Frequent strings earn their own token. Rare ones are spelled from smaller pieces.
02_tokenizer.predict: Which will be split into more pieces: the common word *weather* or the rare word *Reykjavik*? Why?

03_embedding.question: What is an embedding, mechanically?
options: A row looked up in a learned table
A dictionary definition of the word
A compressed copy of the text
03_embedding.why: Token id 559 simply selects row 559 of a 768 by 64 table. Training decides what the numbers are.
03_embedding.predict: If you swapped the vectors for the words *sunny* and *cold*, would the model notice? What does that tell you about where meaning lives?

04_transformer.question: What does each block do to the residual stream?
options: Replaces it with a new one
04_transformer.why: x = x + block(x). Blocks only add. That is what lets gradients flow back through deep stacks.
04_transformer.predict: The transformer has 153,344 numbers. Guess: which part holds the most, the embedding table, attention, or the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP)?

05_attention_closeup.question: Why can a token only attend to tokens before it?
options: When generating, later tokens do not exist yet, so training must not rely on them
05_attention_closeup.why: The causal mask makes training match generation. Otherwise the model would learn to cheat by peeking.
05_attention_closeup.predict: The last token has to start the answer. Which earlier word do you think it will look at hardest: *weather*, *Los*, *Angeles*, or *?*

06_pretraining.question: What labels does pretraining need?
options: None: the next token in real text is the answer key
06_pretraining.why: Next-token prediction is self-supervised. That is why it scales to enormous amounts of text.
06_pretraining.predict: Nobody wrote 'Los Angeles is sunny' as a labelled fact. How could a model learn it just by guessing the next word?

07_backpropagation.question: Why use backpropagation instead of wiggling each weight to see what happens?
options: One backward pass yields every gradient; wiggling needs two forward passes per weight
07_backpropagation.why: Both give the same numbers. The tests in this repository check exactly that. Backpropagation is just vastly cheaper.
07_backpropagation.predict: Suppose you wanted to know how each of the 153,344 weights affects the loss. How many times would you have to run the model if you tested them one at a time?

08_alignment.question: What changes between the base model and the aligned model?
options: Only the weight values, nudged by further training on conversations and preferences
08_alignment.why: Same code, same shapes. Alignment changes behaviour by continuing to train the same weights on different data.
08_alignment.predict: Same weights, same code. What could possibly change a model that rambles into one that answers?

09_sampling.question: With temperature set to 0, asking the same question twice gives...
options: The same answer: it always takes the top token
09_sampling.why: Randomness only enters at the sampling step. Temperature 0 removes it. Try it with the slider above.
09_sampling.predict: If you ask the same question twice, do you get the same answer? What would make it different?

10_output.question: How does the model know when to stop?
options: It predicts a special end token, learned during alignment
10_output.why: The end token is a token like any other. Alignment data taught the model that answers finish with it.
10_output.predict: The answer is 16 tokens long. How many times does the whole model run to produce it?
